name: Dayak (Ngaju)
catalog_quote: Jedes Wort hat nur auf einer Sylbe den Accent. Derselbe fällt, wie die vielen oben angegebenen Beispiele zeigen, auf die vorletzte Sylbe, die ja auch in der Regel die Hauptsylbe des Stammwortes ist. Wo indess, in durch Suffixe abgeleiteten Wörtern, diese Hauptsylbe zur drittletzten Sylbe wird, bleibt der Accent doch auf der Penultima

audit.action: cite a better source for the same coding
audit.reasoning: Both deciding quotations are verbatim in held files at the cited places (Hardeland 1858:18-19, confirmed by page marker and heading; Mihing & Stokhof 1977:55 sec. 3.3.3, confirmed by re-scanned of the held scan's page 7 showing folio 55). The classification rests on the language's only full reference grammar plus an independent 1977 phonology article on a named dialect, 120 years apart, agreeing on penultimate, non-contrastive stress; the database entries (StressTyp2, Gordon 2002) derive from the same 1977 article we hold. Nothing better exists in Glottolog's list: the openly available Indonesian sketches (1991, 2013, fetched sources now) are silent or confused on stress, and Ristati 2006 is an unpublished MA thesis. sources.quote: "In phonemic transcription the place of stress is not indicated because it is not functional. According to our investigation the place of the stress is on the penultimate syllable except when followed by the third person singular possessive marker or/and a place/time marker. In this case stress remains on the penultimate syllable of the word base: ['anak-] 'child'; ['anakah, 'anakeh] 'his child'; ['anakahtE?, 'anakehtE?] 'that child of his'" (Mihing & Stokhof 1977:55, section 3.3.3). Also p. 57,

sources.citation: Hardeland, August. 1858. Versuch einer Grammatik der dajackschen Sprache (Amsterdam: Frederik Muller), section "Accent oder Betonung", pp. 18-19 — read via the full scanned text downloaded from archive.org item bub_gb_xu4UAAAAYAAJ (https://archive.org/download/bub_gb_xu4UAAAAYAAJ/bub_gb_xu4UAAAAYAAJ_dj…
sources.quote: "Every word has the accent on only one syllable. It falls, as the many examples given above show, on the penultimate syllable, which as a rule is also the main syllable of the stem word. Where, however, in words derived by suffixes this main syllable becomes the antepenult, the accent nevertheless remains on the penultima, thus shifting from the originally stressed syllable onto the (formerly) unstressed syllable of the stem." sources.quote: 'It is unclear whether many Malayic languages of Borneo and Sumatra also belong to this type. Ngaju Dayak in Central Kalimantan, impressionistically, at least, appears to show remarkably even prominence across syllables.' One hedged auditory impression, no data; raises the possibility that Ngaju patterns with stressless Indonesian/Javanese rather than fixed penult.
